transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-10 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (Hawthorn VP Eng), Priya Rao (Hawthorn Head ML), Samir Patel (Infra), Lena Ortiz (FinOps)

Summary (auto): quick cost/unit deep-dive focused on batching and KV caching levers; customer has constrained monthly spend (~$30k) and wants guidance on hosted vs reserved/dedicated options for predictable unit cost and latency SLOs; agreed to share sample traffic and run a short benchmark.

00:00 Maya: alright thanks everyone for joining, we, uh, we wanted to keep this tight — focus on the per-token economics and the batching/cache knobs you can use, and then scope a pilot.
00:12 Oliver: perfect yeah, we have like a hard budget band from finance — Lena can confirm — about 30k a month for the initial rollout.
00:18 Lena: yep thats right, 30k target for month one, maybe scale up if results look good, but we need predictable unit costs.
00:27 Priya: our main QA is latency — customer-facing chat median should be under ~300ms P50, but 95th can be higher; we also need to know data residency and KMS support.
00:40 Maya: got it, so three constraints: budget, latency P50 ~300ms, and security (KMS + SOC2). We'll walk through hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs for those.
00:52 Ethan: quick callout on some naming — when I say KV cache I mean the attention KV cache at the runtime layer (not key management), sometimes transcripts write 'K V cash' so just flagging.
01:02 Oliver: hahaha yes we've seen that. Also curious how batching window impacts latency vs token cost with real chat workloads — our messages are small but high QPS spikes during business hours.
01:18 Ethan: right. So fundamentally there's a trade: larger batch windows or continuous batching lower tokens-per-second cost by filling GPU work, but they can increase median latency depending on your SLO. We often recommend adaptive batching with a max wait (e.g., 10ms) to keep P50 tight and still capture batch efficiency.
01:40 Priya: can you ballpark numbers? like if we do adaptive batching vs naive single-request?
01:46 Maya: sure — rough example using a 7B-ish open model: single-request path on hosted (no batching) might be $0.0009/token-equivalent on our list price, whereas with batching and prefix caching you can drive that down 20-40% depending on hit-rate. For our dedicated reserved pricing we give a lower per-token effective price because you commit capacity, so you might average $0.0005-$0.0007/token at scale. (numbers are illustrative)
02:14 Lena: ok so if we have 200M tokens/month target, the delta is real — at 200M tokens, 0.0009 per token is 180k, which is above budget; 0.0006 is 120k, still high. So our 30k/mo means we need a much lower per-token effective cost, or heavy caching.
02:33 Maya: absolutely. That's why batching plus prefix (KV) cache and request routing are critical. If you can hit, say, 50% effective cache hit on prefixes and use batching to raise GPU utilization, your apparent cost per end-user token can drop dramatically. Also model choice matters — smaller distilled models for routing cheap calls, larger models behind a fallback for quality.
02:55 Samir: for us, private deployment is interesting because of data isolation and egress control, but our infra team is small — we can't manage GPU fleets. Is Redwood's private option fully managed?
03:07 Maya: private (VPC) has two flavors: "Redwood-managed private" where we run control plane but you get VPC peering and KMS integration, and "customer-managed on-prem" where we provide a package you install. For smaller infra teams we generally recommend the managed VPC path. Both support KMS and audit logs; SOC2 docs are standard.
03:26 Oliver: what's the SLA like for dedicated vs hosted? We need predictable tails.
03:31 Maya: dedicated reserved pools have SLA-backed latency and throughput targets — and you get capacity isolation which reduces noisy-neighbor tail latencies. Hosted has best-effort latency targets but with routing and fallback policies you can keep apps online. For strict enterprise tails we recommend dedicated or managed private.
03:46 Priya: one concern — when you say "cache hit" do you mean full output cache or KV prefix? Our prompts vary but often share prefixes (policy text + user message).
03:57 Ethan: we mean KV prefix caching + partial response caching. Full output cache works well for identical inputs; prefix/KV cache accelerates autoregressive decoding by restoring key/values. For chat with repeated system prompts and short user messages, KV cache hit rates can be decent.
04:15 Oliver: do you have tooling to estimate a realistic cache hit rate given our prompt templates?
04:21 Maya: yes we have an Optimize tool that analyzes prompt sets and suggests quantization/batching profiles and expected cache hit simulations — but it needs sample logs. That's why we asked for 48-hour samples.
04:32 Lena: we can provide that. But again, finance wants the numbers up front — can you show a pilot that keeps us under 30k for month one?
04:41 Maya: a constrained pilot is doable if we design it: a routing mix that sends 60% of traffic to a distilled hosted model, 30% to a mid-tier model with caching, and 10% to a high-quality fallback. With batch config and a 50% prefix hit, you might hit an effective blended cost within your band for a short pilot; but we should run the benchmark to validate.
05:03 Priya: what's the burst behavior? we have spikes 2x baseline for 20-minute windows.
05:09 Ethan: we have burst capacity on Dedicated and Hosted. On Dedicated you can pre-config burst lanes; on hosted we use smart routing and autoscaling plus a fallback to cheaper model variants to preserve availability. If you need hard latency guarantees under spikes, dedicated with reserved burst is safest.
05:25 Samir: network/residency: we need regionally isolated compute in EU for some lines. Do you do regional private clusters?
05:32 Maya: yes, we can pin deployments to regions and we support EU-only VPCs for private deployments. KMS integrations work with customer keyrings in those regions.
05:41 Oliver: can you explain the tradeoff between quantization and latency/quality? We heard quantized models can lower cost but hurt quality on our tasks.
05:49 Ethan: sure — 8-bit or 4-bit quantization reduces memory and can increase batch density, lowering cost and increasing throughput; quality drip depends on model architecture and prompts. We often recommend running evals on canonical prompts. Quant + distillation + routing can give best of both worlds.
06:05 Maya: note there's also kernel selection and runtime optimizations — some models respond better to certain kernel stacks which affects latency not just raw FLOPS.
06:15 Priya: good — so next step we'd share prompts and logs, you run a benchmark, and then we decide hosted pilot vs reserved capacity?
06:22 Maya: yes. Also we will send a simple worksheet that maps traffic mix -> expected token burn -> suggested configuration (batch window, max batch size, cache TTL, model routing).

-- Transcript middle (times jump a bit, less dense) --
15:05 Oliver: quick procurement question: if we go dedicated reserved, what's the minimum term?
15:12 Maya: typically 3-6 months for pilot contracts, enterprise terms vary. Reserved capacity gets a discount in exchange for commit. We can do month-to-month pilot at a smaller committed pool.
15:23 Lena: finance prefers shorter initial contract.
15:27 Maya: we can structure pilot with a small reserved box and overage pricing to keep predictability.

20:40 Priya: technical deep dive — Ethan, can you sketch the benchmark you plan to run?
20:45 Ethan: sure. We'll take the canonical prompt set and traffic shape, replay 10k requests with real inter-arrival times, measure P50/P95 latency, GPU utilization, token/sec, and cache hit rates. We'll test three configurations: hosted adaptive batching + caching, dedicated reserved with smaller batch windows optimized for latency, and mixed routing (distilled + fallback). We'll collect logs and a small spreadsheet of unit economics.
20:59 Priya: sounds good. Also please include measurements on memory pressure and KV cache effectiveness (hit vs miss) per sequence length.
21:07 Ethan: yes, we'll include cache TTL experiments and a histogram of prompt lengths.

29:12 Oliver: question — how do we instrument cost attribution per feature (search vs chat vs embeddings)? We want token-level tagging so product can bill internally.
29:20 Maya: you can attach route keys and token tags to requests; Console provides token-level cost breakdowns per route/model and per API key. We can also integrate with your internal billing spreadsheet if you want.
29:33 Samir: SSO/SAML and RBAC — is that included?
29:37 Maya: yes, Enterprise includes SAML SSO, granular RBAC, and audit logs shipped to your SIEM.
29:43 Lena: can you share SOC2 and penetration test reports?
29:46 Maya: yes we'll attach the SOC2 report and a pen-test summary in the followups.

35:01 Priya: a bit worried about hallucinations on distill models for policy text — we can't afford a hallucinated policy answer. How do you mitigate?
35:09 Ethan: that is a quality control problem — we recommend routing policy-critical prompts to the high-quality model and adding deterministic checks (heuristics + rules) and a small eval harness to detect regressions. Also can set a higher safety-scoring threshold for those routes.
35:25 Priya: ok. So routing rules + evals + fallback.
35:29 Maya: exactly. We'll propose a pilot routing mix in the worksheet.

43:05 Oliver: final recap?
43:08 Maya: recap: 1) Hawthorn to send 48-hour sample traffic + canonical prompt set by 2026-08-12. 2) Redwood SE to run 10k replay benchmark across three configs and share latency and unit economics by 2026-08-17. 3) Redwood AE to share pilot pricing worksheet, SOC2 and pen-test docs by 2026-08-14. 4) Schedule pilot scoping call week of 2026-08-17.
43:32 Lena: that timeline works. Finance will review the worksheet and flag if we need different structure.
43:38 Oliver: thanks everyone. Quick note — we're also talking to an internal team that is evaluating self-host; we'll need to show the manageability win.
43:47 Maya: understood — we'll include ops overhead estimates and an apples-to-apples cost comparison.
43:53 Priya: ok thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
